report:
Based on my research, here's an evidence summary:

**Report**

The evidence supports a cautious "yes, likely" rather than a definitive "yes." Whole-body vibration (WBV) therapy has been shown to modestly increase bone mineral density (BMD), particularly at the lumbar spine, in postmenopausal and elderly populations, with the strongest effects seen using high-frequency, low-magnitude protocols with high cumulative dose (Springer/Osteoporosis International meta-analysis, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00198-022-06556-y; PMC systematic review, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6112924/). Improved BMD is a recognized proxy for reduced fracture risk, but BMD gains alone don't prove fewer fractures occur.

Direct evidence on actual fracture prevention is more limited. A 2017 systematic review and meta-analysis in BMJ Open (https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/7/12/e018342) found WBV reduced the number of "fallers" and fall rates significantly, and suggested WBV "may prevent fractures by reducing falls," but the number of RCTs reporting actual fracture outcomes was small, limiting statistical power and certainty.

More recent critical commentary (2025, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13643-025-02946-5) pushes back, noting that even the falls-prevention evidence is only moderate-certainty and urging caution before recommending WBV broadly, given trial heterogeneity, small sample sizes, and variable vibration protocols (frequency, amplitude, duration).

**Conclusion:** WBV appears to increase bone density and may indirectly lower fracture risk by reducing falls, but robust RCT evidence directly proving fewer fractures in osteoporosis patients is still lacking. It's a promising adjunct therapy—not yet a proven fracture-prevention intervention—so "yes" is defensible but should be qualified as preliminary/moderate-certainty rather than conclusive.
